slides.title: Two companies
slides.subtitle: Ledgerly pays Ada's invoices at Northwind Bank, by composing two PAP relationships
slides.notes: Ledgerly, an accounting firm, pays Ada's supplier invoices from her account at Northwind Bank. This example shows how one company can act for a user at another, using nothing but ordinary PAP.

slides.title: Composition, not a new protocol
slides.statement: Draft 0.3 defines **no company-to-company protocol**. Two ordinary PAP relationships, for the same user, are enough.
slides.notes: There is no special protocol between companies. Ledgerly is a company to Ada's personal agent, and, separately, a personal agent at Northwind for the same Ada, with its own client_id and keys on its own domain.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph ADA["Ada's side"] direction TB U["Ada"] -- "approves" --> A["Atlas
her personal agent"] end subgraph LED["Ledgerly"] direction TB LC["Company to Atlas"] -- "relays" --> LA["Agent at Northwind
own client_id, keys"] end subgraph NW["Northwind Bank"] direction TB N["Bank API
proposes payments"] end ADA -- "PAP, as to any company" --> LED LED -- "PAP, as any agent" --> NW ADA -. "summaries, who approved" .-> M
slides.caption: Two ordinary PAP relationships meet in Ledgerly; there is no company-to-company protocol.
slides.notes: Read left to right. On Ada's side, Atlas is her personal agent, and to Atlas, Ledgerly is a company like any other. Inside Ledgerly there are two roles: the company Atlas talks to, and a personal agent at Northwind Bank, with its own client_id and keys on its own domain. Northwind only ever sees a personal agent called Ledgerly, which Ada connected herself by approving its code on Northwind's own page. Off to the side, the model receives the companies' summaries and who approved each payment, never a token, code or proof of any party.

slides.title: The first payment
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  actor Ada
  participant A as Atlas
  participant L as Ledgerly
  participant N as Northwind
  L->>N: Pay INV-0042
  N-->>L: Operation n_1, EUR 1250.00
  L-->>A: Operation l_1, quoting n_1
  Ada->>A: Approve l_1
  A->>L: Message with the approval of l_1
  L->>N: n_1 unchanged? Message with the approval of n_1
  N-->>L: Sent, NW-0001
  L-->>A: Northwind's words, as written
slides.notes: Ledgerly asks Northwind to pay the invoice, and Northwind proposes an Operation. Ledgerly relays it to Atlas as its own Operation, quoting Northwind's as written. Ada approves; Ledgerly checks Northwind's revision and terms have not changed, sends the approval of that exact revision, and relays what Northwind says it came to.

slides.title: Every approval is an Operation
slides.statement: Never a chat message, and **Ada is asked about every payment**.
slides.notes: Approving money movement in a chat message would be too easy to fake or misread. In this example every approval is an Operation with a summary and terms the user approves, and draft 0.3 asks the user about each one.

slides.title: Every payment, asked

items.title: INV-0042
items.detail: EUR 1250.00: Ada approves, Northwind sends it

items.title: "Without asking"
items.detail: Ada asks: Ledgerly tells her it cannot

items.title: INV-0043
items.detail: EUR 980.00: a new Operation for Ada

slides.notes: Ada approves the first payment. She then asks Ledgerly to pay Acme without asking her each time, and the answer is no: every operation Northwind returns goes to Ada, and nothing approves one in her name. So the next bill, INV-0043, is a new Operation for her to approve.

slides.title: How Ledgerly approves
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR N["Northwind proposes"] --> O["Operation for Ada"] O -- "Ada approves" --> U["Revision and terms
unchanged?"] U -- "yes" --> C["Sends Northwind
the approval"] O -- "Ada declines" --> X["Nothing is paid"]
slides.caption: Ledgerly approves at Northwind only the exact revision Ada approved.
slides.notes: Follow one Northwind proposal. Ledgerly proposes an Operation for Ada, which Atlas shows with its summary and terms, as it would for any company. If Ada declines, nothing is paid. When Ada approves, Ledgerly checks that Northwind's revision and terms have not changed, and only then sends Northwind the approval of that revision. Northwind's records keep the revision approved and when, and Ledgerly relays what Northwind says it came to, as written.

slides.title: What the model sees

left.heading: Visible
items: Summaries, as the companies wrote them
That there is no company-to-company protocol

slides.notes: The model can explain what happened and who approved it. It never sees a token, code or proof belonging to any of the three parties.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples run all three parties in one process
slides.notes: The same world runs in the SDK's two-companies test. Read the Operations guide for approvals, and the company guide to build either side.
